Reaction orders connect structure to dynamics

A circuit's reaction orders reveal how it returns, adapts, switches and oscillates. Binding and conservation tell us which orders the circuit can attain.

CCBS · Lecture 11 · core · 15 October 2026 · 10:40–12:15

Lecture 10 found adaptation inside nonlinear rate laws. In the incoherent feedforward loop, the input increases both output production and output removal. Their effects cancel at steady state when the reaction orders match. Binding-catalysis supplies that match only within a suitable concentration regime. This raises a broader question: how much of a circuit's behavior can we understand from its reaction orders?

We will connect molecular structure to function in two steps. First, take the rate laws as given and ask what their orders imply for dynamics. Then return to binding-catalysis and calculate the attainable orders. Lectures 8 and 9 provide the molecular allocations and dynamical behaviors. Here we build the link between them.

1Reaction orders provide an intermediate description between molecular structure and dynamical function.

Four parts, nine main sections. Use the tabs to compare views of one example. Present, or the P key, switches to the graphical lecture. Reading mode includes the derivations and assumptions. Open the optional closing comparison before switching to Present to include its animated illustrations.

Part 1

From reaction orders to local dynamics

Define the slopes, compare absolute and relative linearizations, then separate the sign of return from its speed.

1Reaction orders extend mass-action exponents to composite rates

We need a quantity that describes how a rate responds to a concentration change. For an elementary reaction, the exponent already answers that question. A logarithmic derivative extends the same idea to a composite rate that bends as molecules redistribute.

An elementary mass-action reaction has constant orders. Let xix_i denote the concentration of species XiX_i. If reaction jj consumes αij\alpha_{ij} molecules of each species, its mass-action rate is

∑iαijXi→kjproducts,vj(x)=kj∏ixiαij.\sum_i\alpha_{ij}X_i\xrightarrow{k_j}\text{products},\qquad v_j(x)=k_j\prod_i x_i^{\alpha_{ij}}.

The nonnegative integer αij\alpha_{ij} is the reaction order with respect to xix_i. Holding the other species and kjk_j fixed, doubling xix_i multiplies the rate by 2αij2^{\alpha_{ij}}. The units of kjk_j make vjv_j a concentration per unit time.

A composite catalytic flux responds to total concentrations. Recall the resolved enzyme mechanism and its instantaneous catalytic flux:

E+S⇌k−k+CES→kcatE+P,v=kcatCES.E+S\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{ES}\xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{cat}}}E+P,\qquad v=k_{\mathrm{cat}}C_{ES}.

Let qE=E+CESq_E=E+C_{ES} denote total enzyme and qS=S+CESq_S=S+C_{ES} total unconverted substrate. Assume binding equilibrates much faster than catalysis, with Kd=k−/k+K_d=k_-/k_+. In the trace-enzyme limit, bound substrate is negligible compared with the substrate total. A sufficient condition is qE≪qSq_E\ll q_S. Then S≈qSS\approx q_S and

v(qE,qS)≈kcatqEqSKd+qS.v(q_E,q_S)\approx k_{\mathrm{cat}}q_E\frac{q_S}{K_d+q_S}.

This is an effective rate law for the composite conversion S⇝PS\rightsquigarrow P. Its substrate dependence changes continuously between the unsaturated and saturated regimes.

2A composite reaction order is the local slope of its rate on logarithmic axes.

Define the slope before interpreting it. For a positive flux vv and positive independent total qiq_i, hold the other independent totals and all parameters fixed. Define the reaction order

Hv←qi:=∂log⁡v∂log⁡qi=qiv∂v∂qi.H^{v\leftarrow q_i}:=\frac{\partial\log v}{\partial\log q_i}=\frac{q_i}{v}\frac{\partial v}{\partial q_i}.

The reaction order is dimensionless. An order of two means that a small one-percent input increase produces about a two-percent rate increase. For a monomial, the derivative equals the exponent. For a general composite rate, it depends on the state. Logarithms here and below use fixed reference units. The derivative is independent of those units.

Saturation lowers the substrate order from one toward zero. Differentiating the trace-enzyme rate law gives

Hv←qS=KdKd+qS.H^{v\leftarrow q_S}=\frac{K_d}{K_d+q_S}.

A local slope predicts nearby fold changes. Using one exponent over a finite range requires the order to stay nearly constant there. Dominance regimes provide that reason. This is how Lecture 9's changes in molecular allocation become changes in regulatory behavior.

Read an elementary exponent and a composite logarithmic slope as the same response quantity. State the input, held-fixed quantities and concentration range before using either.

Turn rate responses into a statement about the motion of the state.

2Addition and removal orders give the relative linearization

Ordinary linearization describes small absolute displacements. In biomolecular systems we also care about relative concentration changes. Comparing the two descriptions reveals where reaction orders enter the dynamics.

Start with the familiar linearization. For x˙=f(x)\dot x=f(x), choose a fixed point f(x∗)=0f(x^*)=0 and a small displacement δx=x−x∗\delta x=x-x^*. Taylor expansion gives the first-order system

δx˙=Aδx,A=Df(x∗).\dot{\delta x}=A\delta x,\qquad A=Df(x^*).

The Jacobian AA determines local return or departure. A matrix is Hurwitz when all its eigenvalues have negative real part. A Hurwitz Jacobian gives local asymptotic stability of the fixed point. Eigenvalues on the imaginary axis require further analysis.

Biomolecular dynamics have addition and removal structure. Write the slow total-concentration dynamics as q˙=f(q)=Sv(q)\dot q=f(q)=Sv(q), with slow stoichiometric matrix SS. Group the positive and negative contributions in each row:

fi(q)=fi+(q)−fi−(q),fi+=∑Sij>0Sijvj,fi−=−∑Sij<0Sijvj.f_i(q)=f_i^+(q)-f_i^-(q),\qquad f_i^+=\sum_{S_{ij}>0}S_{ij}v_j,\qquad f_i^-=-\sum_{S_{ij}<0}S_{ij}v_j.

Choose independent dynamical totals after removing fixed conservation constraints. At the reference fixed point, assume qi∗>0q_i^*>0 and positive balanced fluxes fi+(q∗)=fi−(q∗)=:fi∗>0f_i^+(q^*)=f_i^-(q^*)=:f_i^*>0. This balance lets us factor the same reference flux out of both derivatives.

Define how each aggregate flux responds to relative changes. The addition-order matrix and removal-order matrix, evaluated at the reference fixed point, are

Hij+=∂log⁡fi+∂log⁡qj∣q∗,Hij−=∂log⁡fi−∂log⁡qj∣q∗,H:=H+−H−.H^+_{ij}=\left.\frac{\partial\log f_i^+}{\partial\log q_j}\right|_{q^*},\qquad H^-_{ij}=\left.\frac{\partial\log f_i^-}{\partial\log q_j}\right|_{q^*},\qquad H:=H^+-H^-.

We call HH the balance-order matrix. Its entries compare the fractional responses of addition and removal. If an aggregate flux contains several terms, its order is their flux-weighted average. Constant elementary orders therefore need not give a constant aggregate order.

Rewrite the ordinary Jacobian using those orders. For the total-concentration system, A=Df(q∗)A=Df(q^*). The logarithmic derivative gives ∂fi±/∂qj=(fi∗/qj∗)Hij±\partial f_i^\pm/\partial q_j=(f_i^*/q_j^*)H^\pm_{ij}. Subtracting the two contributions yields

Aij=fi∗qj∗Hij,δq˙i=∑jfi∗qj∗Hijδqj.A_{ij}=\frac{f_i^*}{q_j^*}H_{ij},\qquad \dot{\delta q}_i=\sum_j\frac{f_i^*}{q_j^*}H_{ij}\delta q_j.

Relative displacements reveal the turnover factor. Define zqi:=δqi/qi∗=(qi−qi∗)/qi∗z_{q_i}:=\delta q_i/q_i^*=(q_i-q_i^*)/q_i^*, and collect these components in zqz_q. For small changes, zqiz_{q_i} agrees to first order with log⁡(qi/qi∗)\log(q_i/q_i^*). Substitute δqj=qj∗zqj\delta q_j=q_j^*z_{q_j} and divide row ii by qi∗q_i^*:

z˙qi=1qi∗∑jfi∗qj∗Hijqj∗zqj=fi∗qi∗∑jHijzqj.\dot z_{q_i}=\frac{1}{q_i^*}\sum_j\frac{f_i^*}{q_j^*}H_{ij}q_j^*z_{q_j}=\frac{f_i^*}{q_i^*}\sum_jH_{ij}z_{q_j}.

The turnover time measures how long the steady flux takes to replace a pool. Define τi∗:=qi∗/fi∗\tau_i^*:=q_i^*/f_i^*. For any vector aa, write Λa=diag⁡(a)\Lambda_a=\operatorname{diag}(a). The matrix form is

z˙q=Λτ∗−1Hzq,Λτ∗=diag⁡(τi∗).\boxed{\dot z_q=\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H z_q,\qquad\Lambda_{\tau^*}=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_i^*).}

The inverse is essential: a dimensionless order must multiply a reciprocal time. The two linearizations are related by the diagonal change of coordinates δq=Λq∗zq\delta q=\Lambda_{q^*}z_q:

δq˙=Aδq⏟absolute displacement⟷z˙q=Λτ∗−1Hzq⏟relative displacement,A=Λq∗Λτ∗−1HΛq∗−1.\underbrace{\dot{\delta q}=A\delta q}_{\text{absolute displacement}}\qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad\underbrace{\dot z_q=\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H z_q}_{\text{relative displacement}},\qquad A=\Lambda_{q^*}\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H\Lambda_{q^*}^{-1}.

A monomial regime keeps the orders fixed while the clocks vary. Kinetic constants can change steady concentrations and turnover times without changing monomial exponents. This makes the balance-order matrix a useful description of structure. Outside a fixed-order regime, parameters can also change the orders, so the separation is conditional.1

Linearize in relative concentrations to obtain Λτ∗−1H\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H. The same eigenvalues govern the absolute linearization, while the order matrix and turnover times become visible separately.

3One balance order separates stability from speed

One pool makes the separation between location, stability and speed visible. The rate intersection tells us where the state is. The balance order tells us whether nearby states return. The turnover time tells us how fast.

Take constant addition and first-order removal. Let μ>0\mu>0 be an addition flux and λ>0\lambda>0 a removal rate constant:

q˙=μ−λq,q∗=μ/λ.\dot q=\mu-\lambda q,\qquad q^*=\mu/\lambda.

Addition has order zero in qq. Removal has order one. Their difference is H=−1H=-1. At the intersection, the turnover time is τ∗=q∗/μ=1/λ\tau^*=q^*/\mu=1/\lambda. Therefore

z˙q=−zq/τ∗,zq(t)=zq(0)e−t/τ∗.\dot z_q=-z_q/\tau^*,\qquad z_q(t)=z_q(0)e^{-t/\tau^*}.

3Changing a positive turnover time changes the speed of return, while the negative balance order preserves stability.

For one positive balanced pool, a negative balance order gives local return for every positive turnover time. A positive balance order gives local departure.

Ask the same robustness question for coupled pools.

Part 2

Structural stability and adaptation

Ask which local behaviors survive changing turnover times. Test return with the state orders and adaptation with the input-output orders.

4A diagonal certificate makes stability independent of turnover times

Molecular lifetimes can differ widely. We want a stability statement that survives those differences. The question is now whether every positive row scaling of the same balance-order matrix remains stable.

Define the robustness property precisely. A matrix HH is D-stable if DHDH is Hurwitz for every positive diagonal matrix DD. For our circuit, this means local stability for every positive vector of turnover times, while the balance-order matrix stays fixed. Stability of HH alone does not establish this property.

A diagonal quadratic certificate is a sufficient test. Look for a positive diagonal matrix P=diag⁡(pi)P=\operatorname{diag}(p_i) such that

P≻0,PH+HTP≺0.P\succ0,\qquad PH+H^{\mathsf T}P\prec0.

The second inequality means negative definiteness: every nonzero vector gives a negative quadratic form. Existence of this certificate is called diagonal stability. Diagonal stability implies D-stability. It is a sufficient condition, not an equivalent definition in general. For a specified matrix, the certificate can be sought through a linear matrix inequality.1

4A single negative quadratic form certifies return for every positive turnover time.

The certificate works because the turnover times cancel in the decay calculation. Choose a weighted squared perturbation V(zq)=zqTΛτ∗PzqV(z_q)=z_q^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_{\tau^*}Pz_q. It is positive away from zero. Along the linearized dynamics,

V˙=zqT(HTP+PH)zq<0(zq≠0).\dot V=z_q^{\mathsf T}(H^{\mathsf T}P+PH)z_q\lt0\qquad(z_q\ne0).

Apply the certificate within its regime. A positive equilibrium must exist, and its balance-order matrix must be the stated HH. Regime conditions identify the parameter choices that preserve these hypotheses. A parameter change that leaves the regime calls for a new balance-order matrix and a new stability check.

To certify local stability independently of positive turnover times, find a positive diagonal PP with PH+HTP≺0PH+H^{\mathsf T}P\prec0, then check that the proposed state has that balance-order matrix.

5One certificate handles a six-species circuit

The scalar example could be checked by inspection. The benefit of the certificate is that the calculation can stay short when many species interact. This illustrative circuit has both positive and negative influences around a ring.

Specify a monomial regime for six independent totals. Let the indices wrap around the ring, so q0=q6q_0=q_6 and q7=q1q_7=q_1. Take positive constants ai,bia_i,b_i and composite addition and removal laws

q˙i=aiqi−1−biqiqi+1,i=1,…,6.\dot q_i=a_iq_{i-1}-b_iq_iq_{i+1},\qquad i=1,\ldots,6.

The predecessor increases addition. The successor increases removal. The constants have units of inverse time and inverse concentration per time, respectively. These are effective laws in a stated monomial regime, rather than an assertion that the whole biological process is one elementary reaction.

Read the balance-order matrix directly from the exponents. Its diagonal entries are minus one. The predecessor contributes plus one and the successor minus one. Let RR be the cyclic matrix defined by (Rzq)i=zqi−1(Rz_q)_i=z_{q_{i-1}}. Then

H=−I+R−RT,H+HT=−2I.H=-I+R-R^{\mathsf T},\qquad H+H^{\mathsf T}=-2I.

5The opposing cross influences cancel in the symmetric part. Self-removal supplies the negative remainder.

The choice P=IP=I certifies diagonal stability immediately. Every positive steady state of this monomial model is therefore locally stable for every positive turnover-time vector. No symbolic sixth-degree root calculation is needed.

The leading model also has a unique positive candidate. Write the steady equations in logarithms using a reference concentration qrefq_{\mathrm{ref}}. Since the certificate makes HH nonsingular,

Hlog⁡(q∗/qref)=(log⁡biqrefai)i=16H\log(q^*/q_{\mathrm{ref}})=\left(\log\frac{b_iq_{\mathrm{ref}}}{a_i}\right)_{i=1}^6

has one solution, and exponentiating gives positive concentrations. A biochemical implementation must still place those concentrations in the regime that justifies the monomial laws. This last check will matter when several regimes are possible.

For a large circuit, look for a simple symmetric-part calculation before expanding a characteristic polynomial. Keep equilibrium feasibility and regime validity as separate checks.

A stable circuit can still transmit a persistent disturbance. Now test the output.

6Input-output order cancellation gives adaptation

Stability tells us that the state returns to an equilibrium. Adaptation asks whether that equilibrium restores the output after an input change. The familiar input-output linearization gives us a direct parallel for the reaction-order calculation.

Recall the four matrices of a classical control system. Let x˙=f(x,w)\dot x=f(x,w) and y=h(x,w)y=h(x,w), with scalar input ww and scalar output yy. Hold the input at w∗w^* and choose a fixed point f(x∗,w∗)=0f(x^*,w^*)=0. Define y∗=h(x∗,w∗)y^*=h(x^*,w^*). Small absolute displacements satisfy

δx˙=Aδx+bδw,δy=cδx+dδw,\dot{\delta x}=A\delta x+b\delta w,\qquad\delta y=c\delta x+d\delta w,
A=∂f∂x,b=∂f∂w,c=∂h∂x,d=∂h∂w,A=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\qquad b=\frac{\partial f}{\partial w},\qquad c=\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\qquad d=\frac{\partial h}{\partial w},

with derivatives evaluated at (x∗,w∗)(x^*,w^*). Here cc is a row vector. If AA is nonsingular, a constant input displacement gives δy∗=(d−cA−1b)δw\delta y^*=(d-cA^{-1}b)\delta w. Stability supplies convergence to that new fixed point.

Now use the positive flux structure of a biomolecular system. Write q˙=f+(q,w)−f−(q,w)\dot q=f^+(q,w)-f^-(q,w) and y=h(q,w)y=h(q,w). Assume positive totals, positive input, positive balanced addition and removal, and a positive readout near (q∗,w∗)(q^*,w^*). The readout can be a concentration or a flux. Positivity makes its logarithmic derivatives well defined. Set

zq=Λq∗−1δq,zw=δww∗,zy=δyy∗.z_q=\Lambda_{q^*}^{-1}\delta q,\qquad z_w=\frac{\delta w}{w^*},\qquad z_y=\frac{\delta y}{y^*}.

Define four order blocks in the same positions as the four classical matrices. At the reference point,

HA=∂log⁡f+∂log⁡q−∂log⁡f−∂log⁡q=H,Hb=∂log⁡f+∂log⁡w−∂log⁡f−∂log⁡w,Hc=∂log⁡h∂log⁡q,Hd=∂log⁡h∂log⁡w.\begin{aligned}H^A&=\frac{\partial\log f^+}{\partial\log q}-\frac{\partial\log f^-}{\partial\log q}=H,\qquad&H^b&=\frac{\partial\log f^+}{\partial\log w}-\frac{\partial\log f^-}{\partial\log w},\\H^c&=\frac{\partial\log h}{\partial\log q},&H^d&=\frac{\partial\log h}{\partial\log w}.\end{aligned}

The state and input blocks subtract removal orders from addition orders. The output blocks differentiate the positive readout directly. The balance and coordinate change used in section 2 give

z˙q=Λτ∗−1(HAzq+Hbzw),zy=Hczq+Hdzw.\boxed{\dot z_q=\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}(H^A z_q+H^b z_w),\qquad z_y=H^c z_q+H^d z_w.}
RoleAbsolute linearizationRelative linearization
State responseAAΛτ∗−1HA\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H^A
Input responsebbΛτ∗−1Hb\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H^b
Readout of stateccHcH^c
Direct input readoutddHdH^d

Solve the constant-input perturbation to find the steady output response. For nonsingular HAH^A, the steady equation gives zq∗=−(HA)−1Hbzwz_q^*=-(H^A)^{-1}H^b z_w. Thus

dlog⁡y∗dlog⁡w=Hd−Hc(HA)−1Hb.\frac{d\log y^*}{d\log w}=H^d-H^c(H^A)^{-1}H^b.

Input cancellation is a singularity of the full input-output order matrix. The block determinant identity gives

det⁡[HAHbHcHd]=det⁡HA(Hd−Hc(HA)−1Hb).\det\begin{bmatrix}H^A&H^b\\H^c&H^d\end{bmatrix}=\det H^A\bigl(H^d-H^c(H^A)^{-1}H^b\bigr).

The left-hand determinant vanishes exactly when the local steady output response vanishes, provided HAH^A is nonsingular. A stable state block is the additional condition that makes nearby trajectories reach the new equilibrium.1

6Adaptation requires both a stable state and cancellation of the steady input-to-output response.

Apply the test to Lecture 10's incoherent feedforward loop. In the regime where enzyme-mediated removal is bilinear in the relevant totals, take

q˙1=k1w−δq1q2,q˙2=k2w−γq2,y=q1.\dot q_1=k_1w-\delta q_1q_2,\qquad\dot q_2=k_2w-\gamma q_2,\qquad y=q_1.

All constants are positive and carry the units required by these fluxes. In the state order (q1,q2)(q_1,q_2), the two input orders are one, the readout selects q1q_1, and there is no direct input term in the readout. Therefore

HA=(−1−10−1),Hb=(11),Hc=(10),Hd=0.H^A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad H^b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad H^c=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad H^d=0.

The triangular balance-order matrix remains Hurwitz under every positive row scaling. The input-output order matrix has determinant zero. The circuit passes both tests.

The steady balances establish finite-range adaptation for this rate law. They give

q2∗=k2γw,q1∗=k1γδk2.q_2^*=\frac{k_2}{\gamma}w,\qquad q_1^*=\frac{k_1\gamma}{\delta k_2}.

The output is independent of every positive constant ww for which this model applies. Here the finite-range result follows from the exact steady relation. A zero derivative at one point would establish only local insensitivity. If the removal enzyme saturates or substantial binding invalidates the chosen totals law, the orders and adaptation condition must be recalculated.

Use the balance-order matrix to check local return, then use the input-output order matrix to check steady input cancellation. Prove a constant set point separately when claiming adaptation over a finite range.

A regime supplies a candidate state. The candidate still has to belong to that regime.

Part 3

Regime consistency connects local models to global behaviors

Solve the leading balances and check their validity. Consistent candidates support stable states. Inconsistent candidates can organize regime transitions.

7Stable candidates must satisfy their regime conditions

A stability certificate tests the balance-order matrix. It does not test whether the equilibrium belongs to the concentration regime that produced that matrix. That second test turns a stable candidate into a possible state of the circuit.

Use the same analysis sequence in every regime. First specify the concentration inequalities. Write the leading rates and solve their balance. Check local stability through the balance-order matrix. Then substitute the candidate into its own regime inequalities. Stable consistent candidates at the same parameter values can coexist. Figures 10 and 11 keep these tasks aligned.3

Monomial balances make candidate concentrations easy to find. Choose fixed reference concentrations and write qˉi=qi/qiref\bar q_i=q_i/q_i^{\mathrm{ref}}. Within one regime, let the leading addition and removal rates be ai∏jqˉjHij+a_i\prod_j\bar q_j^{H^+_{ij}} and bi∏jqˉjHij−b_i\prod_j\bar q_j^{H^-_{ij}}. The positive coefficients ai,bia_i,b_i have the same flux units. At steady balance, taking logarithms gives

Hlog⁡qˉ∗=log⁡(b/a),H=H+−H−.H\log\bar q^*=\log(b/a),\qquad H=H^+-H^-.

When HH is nonsingular, this linear system gives one positive candidate. The regime's concentration inequalities must then be checked at that candidate. A candidate outside those inequalities belongs to the continued monomial model, but does not supply an equilibrium of that regime.

A cooperative autoactivator shows how consistent candidates coexist. One protein activates its own production. A fast cooperative promoter closure gives the composite model

q˙=μ+Vq2K2+q2−λq.\dot q=\mu+V\frac{q^2}{K^2+q^2}-\lambda q.

Here μ\mu is basal production, VV is maximal induced production, KK is the activation concentration, and λ\lambda is the first-order removal constant. The promoter model must justify the Hill exponent two. We now use its limiting rate laws to test bistability.

There are three monomial balances, each with its own validity conditions. Basal production dominates when q≪Kq\ll K and Vq2/K2≪μVq^2/K^2\ll\mu. Unsaturated activation dominates when Kμ/V≪q≪KK\sqrt{\mu/V}\ll q\ll K. Saturated activation applies when q≫Kq\gg K. Balancing each addition law against λq\lambda q gives

qbasal∗=μλ,qunsaturated∗=λK2V,qsaturated∗=μ+Vλ.q_{\mathrm{basal}}^*=\frac{\mu}{\lambda},\qquad q_{\mathrm{unsaturated}}^*=\frac{\lambda K^2}{V},\qquad q_{\mathrm{saturated}}^*=\frac{\mu+V}{\lambda}.

The corresponding scalar balance orders are −1,+1,−1-1,+1,-1. The first and third candidates are structurally stable. The middle candidate is unstable.

7For each candidate, check stability and substitute its concentration into every regime inequality.

μ/(λK)\mu/(\lambda K) = 0.001, V/(λK)V/(\lambda K) = 10. Two stable equilibria and one unstable equilibrium.

Coexistence requires the consistency conditions to hold together. Substituting the three candidates yields a simple sufficient range:

μV≪(λK)2,λK≪V.\mu V\ll(\lambda K)^2,\qquad\lambda K\ll V.

These conditions imply μ≪V\mu\ll V. They place the basal and saturated stable candidates in their own regimes, with an unstable unsaturated candidate between them. For the default bistable parameter choice in Figures 10 and 11, the concentration ordering is

0.001K<0.01K<0.1K<K<10.001K.0.001K<0.01K<0.1K<K<10.001K.

The five levels are the basal candidate, the basal-to-induced crossover, the unsaturated candidate, the activation concentration, and the saturated candidate. The neglected terms produce corrections of about one percent at these candidates.

The full smooth model confirms bistability at this parameter choice. At the default parameters, its equilibrium concentrations are approximately q/K=0.00101, 0.09999, 9.90000q/K=0.00101,\ 0.09999,\ 9.90000. The derivative of addition minus removal is negative at the first and third roots and positive at the middle root. Initial conditions on opposite sides of the middle root approach different stable states. This smooth-model check supplements the leading regime calculation.2

To predict multistability from regimes, find stable candidates whose consistency conditions hold at the same parameter values. Check that the full rate law preserves those states.

What happens when stable leading balances keep pointing outside their own regimes?

8Virtual targets connect regimes in an oscillatory example

A stable monomial balance can pull toward a candidate outside its own regime. As the concentration state leaves that regime, the dominant rate law changes. The repressilator turns this into a cycle of candidate destinations.

Three repressors form a negative-feedback ring. Each protein suppresses production of the next. Use the common repression concentration KK and common turnover time t0t_0 to define qˉi=qi/K\bar q_i=q_i/K and tˉ=t/t0\bar t=t/t_0. The composite model is

dqˉidtˉ=α1+qˉi−1 n−qˉi,i=1,2,3.\frac{d\bar q_i}{d\bar t}=\frac{\alpha}{1+\bar q_{i-1}^{\,n}}-\bar q_i,\qquad i=1,2,3.

Indices wrap around the ring. The parameter α\alpha is maximal production divided by K/t0K/t_0. The Hill exponent nn represents effective cooperativity in a fast regulatory closure. A binding mechanism must justify this closure and its operating range.

High and low concentrations select eight regimes. Write ↑\uparrow for qˉi≫1\bar q_i\gg1 and ↓\downarrow for qˉi≪1\bar q_i\ll1. Tuples always list (q1,q2,q3)(q_1,q_2,q_3). A low repressor gives leading addition α\alpha, with order zero. A high repressor gives leading addition αqˉi−1−n\alpha\bar q_{i-1}^{-n}, with order −n-n. Removal has own-total order one in every regime.

A virtual target is a candidate outside its own regime. Continue the regime's monomial laws beyond their validity range and solve their steady balance. If that candidate violates the regime inequalities, call it a virtual target. We can ask which other regime contains the candidate. This target relation identifies the concentration range toward which the continued model pulls. It does not identify the first boundary crossed by the actual trajectory.

One calculation supplies both stability and a destination. Take n=3n=3, α≫1\alpha\gg1, and the regime (↑,↓,↑)(\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow). Its leading balances and balance-order matrix are

qˉ3∗=α,qˉ1∗=α(qˉ3∗)−3=α−2,qˉ2∗=α(qˉ1∗)−3=α7,H=(−10−3−3−1000−1).\bar q_3^*=\alpha,\qquad\bar q_1^*=\alpha(\bar q_3^*)^{-3}=\alpha^{-2},\qquad\bar q_2^*=\alpha(\bar q_1^*)^{-3}=\alpha^7,\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&-3\\-3&-1&0\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}.

Reordering the species as (q3,q1,q2)(q_3,q_1,q_2) makes HH triangular with negative diagonal entries. Positive turnover scaling preserves those signs. The candidate is therefore locally stable in the continued monomial model. Its concentrations instead satisfy (↓,↑,↑)(\downarrow,\uparrow,\uparrow), so the candidate is a virtual target.

Cyclic relabeling closes the target loop. The three regimes with two high concentrations point to one another. Each of the three regimes with one high concentration has a stable virtual target in that loop. In every mixed regime, a zero regulatory order breaks the leading feedback ring. The resulting triangular balance-order matrix gives stability for every positive turnover scaling.2

The two uniform regimes require separate checks. The all-low regime has H=−IH=-I and candidate qˉ∗=(α,α,α)\bar q^*=(\alpha,\alpha,\alpha). For α≫1\alpha\gg1, that stable candidate lies in the all-high regime. The all-high regime has the consistent candidate qˉi∗=α1/4\bar q_i^*=\alpha^{1/4}. For n=3n=3 and equal clocks, its leading eigenvalues are −4-4 and 1/2±i33/21/2\pm i3\sqrt{3}/2, so the candidate is unstable. Neither uniform regime supplies a stable consistent leading state under these conditions.

8Stable virtual targets form a loop. Check the other regimes and the full dynamics before concluding that the circuit oscillates.

The three two-high regimes form the target loop. The three one-high regimes point into that loop. The all-low candidate points to the all-high regime, whose candidate is unstable for the chosen clocks. This classification identifies no stable consistent leading candidate. It still leaves boundary transitions and the existence of an attracting periodic orbit to be checked.

The finite Hill law supplies the stability check that the regime limits cannot replace. Its unique positive equilibrium is symmetric and satisfies qˉ∗(1+(qˉ∗)n)=α\bar q^*(1+(\bar q^*)^n)=\alpha. Uniqueness follows because three successive repression functions give a strictly decreasing fixed-point map. At that equilibrium, the magnitude of each local production order is

g=n(qˉ∗)n1+(qˉ∗)n.g=\frac{n(\bar q^*)^n}{1+(\bar q^*)^n}.

With equal clocks, the eigenvalues in units of 1/t01/t_0 are −1−g-1-g and −1+g/2±i3g/2-1+g/2\pm i\sqrt{3}g/2. The equilibrium is unstable when g>2g>2. For α=100\alpha=100 and n=3n=3, the equilibrium is approximately 3.14K3.14K and g≈2.91g\approx2.91. The growing oscillatory mode agrees with the strongly repressed leading regime.

The full trajectory establishes an oscillatory example. Direct integration of the smooth rate law produces a repeating trajectory with period about 10.2t010.2t_0. A numerical return calculation finds contraction transverse to the cycle. These calculations use illustrative parameters. The target graph explains the changing dominant balances, while the full dynamical calculation verifies this example.

Weaker repression exposes the limit of the target-loop argument. At n=2n=2, the finite Hill law has g<2g<2 at every finite α\alpha. The symmetric equilibrium is therefore stable for equal clocks, even though the mixed-regime target loop still exists. At α=100\alpha=100, the local magnitude is approximately 1.91 and a small oscillatory perturbation decays. Unequal clocks also require their own stability test.

Regime consistency locates stable states and virtual targets. A target loop organizes possible repeated regime changes. Stability and the full dynamics determine whether those changes sustain an oscillation.

We have used reaction orders to read dynamics. Now derive the orders from binding-catalysis.

Part 4

From binding-catalysis to attainable reaction orders

Close the structure-to-function route by deriving the order constraints, then follow a concentration path through the exact triangle.

9Binding and conservation determine the attainable reaction orders

A holistic account of bioregulation would describe the behaviors a mechanism permits across its concentration and parameter ranges. Solving one trajectory or one equilibrium does not give that account. Reaction orders offer a tractable intermediate object: we can calculate their constraints directly from the binding layer.

Write the binding equilibrium through its defining constraints. Let x>0x>0 list nn free and bound species. Let the mm rows of LL count conserved constituents, so Lx=qLx=q. Choose n−mn-m independent equilibrium relations and write them as

Lx=q,Nlog⁡x=log⁡k.Lx=q,\qquad N\log x=\log k.

Here NN contains the exponents in the independent binding relations. The vector kk contains their compatible equilibrium constants, expressed using fixed reference units. It is not a list of every microscopic kinetic rate constant. As before, Λx=diag⁡(x)\Lambda_x=\operatorname{diag}(x) and Λq=diag⁡(q)\Lambda_q=\operatorname{diag}(q).

Differentiate to obtain the responses without an explicit root formula. Since dx=Λx dlog⁡xdx=\Lambda_x\,d\log x and dq=Λq dlog⁡qdq=\Lambda_q\,d\log q, the conservation equations give Λq−1LΛx dlog⁡x=dlog⁡q\Lambda_q^{-1}L\Lambda_x\,d\log x=d\log q. The equilibrium equations give N dlog⁡x=dlog⁡kN\,d\log x=d\log k. Stack the two:

[Λq−1LΛxN]dlog⁡x=[dlog⁡qdlog⁡k].\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda_q^{-1}L\Lambda_x\\N\end{bmatrix}d\log x=\begin{bmatrix}d\log q\\d\log k\end{bmatrix}.

9The reaction-order formula is one inverse of the differentiated binding and conservation constraints.

At a positive equilibrium where this square matrix is nonsingular,

∂log⁡x∂log⁡(q,k)=[Λq−1LΛxN]−1.\boxed{\frac{\partial\log x}{\partial\log(q,k)}=\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda_q^{-1}L\Lambda_x\\N\end{bmatrix}^{-1}.}

The formula makes a whole set of possible orders accessible. Vary the admissible positive state xx and evaluate the inverse. Its image is the attainable reaction-order set. With fixed affinities, restrict the states to Nlog⁡x=log⁡kN\log x=\log k. This parametrization can characterize order geometry without first eliminating species into high-degree polynomials and solving explicit equilibrium formulas.

The formula still depends on the state. Finding the equilibrium for one prescribed (q,k)(q,k) may require a numerical solve. The gain is that derivatives and their possible geometry have a direct constraint-based expression. A full classification of attainable orders and global behaviors for general networks remains a research problem.

One binding pair makes the geometry exact and visible. Return to the enzyme-substrate complex, now retaining both conservation laws without the trace-enzyme approximation:

qE=E+CES,qS=S+CES,KdCES=ES,v=kcatCES.q_E=E+C_{ES},\qquad q_S=S+C_{ES},\qquad K_dC_{ES}=ES,\qquad v=k_{\mathrm{cat}}C_{ES}.

At fixed KdK_d, differentiation gives (Kd+E+S)dCES=S dqE+E dqS(K_d+E+S)dC_{ES}=S\,dq_E+E\,dq_S. At fixed kcatk_{\mathrm{cat}}, the catalytic flux has the same orders as the complex:

Hv←qE=Kd+SKd+E+S,Hv←qS=Kd+EKd+E+S.H^{v\leftarrow q_E}=\frac{K_d+S}{K_d+E+S},\qquad H^{v\leftarrow q_S}=\frac{K_d+E}{K_d+E+S}.

The two orders are coupled, rather than chosen independently. Their vector is

(Hv←qEHv←qS)=KdKd+E+S(11)+SKd+E+S(10)+EKd+E+S(01).\begin{pmatrix}H^{v\leftarrow q_E}\\H^{v\leftarrow q_S}\end{pmatrix}=\frac{K_d}{K_d+E+S}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}+\frac{S}{K_d+E+S}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\frac{E}{K_d+E+S}\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}.

The weights are positive and sum to one. The orders therefore lie inside the triangle with corners (1,1)(1,1), (1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1). Every interior point is attainable at fixed positive KdK_d. The edges and corners are limits. Each corner corresponds to a dominant molecular allocation and a limiting catalytic law.1

10As concentrations change, the circuit traces a path through its attainable reaction orders.

This picture connects the end of the lecture to its beginning. A slow trajectory changes the totals, which redistribute bound species and change the composite reaction orders. Those orders enter addition and removal, hence the local balance-order matrix. Adaptation, return, switching and oscillation can be studied through the order structures visited by the circuit.

The geometry constrains dynamics without replacing the dynamics. A path in reaction-order space need not retain the clock or all information about the concentrations. General attainable order sets need not be triangles or even convex. Complete bioregulation still requires feasible states, flux balance, regime transitions and attractor analysis. The inverse formula makes the structure-to-order part analyzable and gives those dynamical questions a common language.

Lecture 12 asks what task these behaviors perform. A stable response can transmit a signal, coexisting states can store a decision, and an oscillation can organize timing. The computation biomachine perspective asks which of these functions a cell uses and how molecular architecture implements it.

Derive reaction orders by differentiating binding and conservation. Use the attainable order set to constrain possible responses, then combine it with flux balance and dynamical tests to establish a function.

A6 · Why degradation and repression adapt in different concentration ranges

One incoherent feedforward loop can fail in opposite directions. Lecture 9 compared degradation of the output with repression of its production. Lecture 10 explained the cancellation in a suitable limiting rate law. We can now test both implementations across their binding regimes. Keep the input positive, the affinities fixed, and the controller's removal rule explicit.

Use the same two slow totals and readout as Lecture 9. The dimensionless input uu drives synthesis. The output is y=qXy=q_X. Controller removal acts at frequency γ\gamma on every controller-containing state. Removing a bound controller releases its partner. Consequently both implementations have q˙Y=k2u−γqY\dot q_Y=k_2u-\gamma q_Y. Binding is equilibrated on the slower synthesis and removal timescale. The equations below retain its full conservation laws.

Degradation removes bound output and returns its controller. Represent bound-output conversion as one modeled catalytic step. Let PP denote untracked degradation products. The resolved binding and catalytic steps are

X+Y⇌k−k+CXY,CXY→kcatY+P.X+Y\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{XY},\qquad C_{XY}\xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{cat}}}Y+P.
q˙X=k1,Du−vD,vD=kcatCXY,qX=X+CXY,qY=Y+CXY,KdCXY=XY.\dot q_X=k_{1,\mathrm D}u-v_{\mathrm D},\quad v_{\mathrm D}=k_{\mathrm{cat}}C_{XY},\quad q_X=X+C_{XY},\quad q_Y=Y+C_{XY},\quad K_dC_{XY}=XY.

The removal flux traces the triangle from section 9. Differentiate the binding balances at fixed KdK_d and kcatk_{\mathrm{cat}}:

HvD←qX=Kd+YKd+X+Y,HvD←qY=Kd+XKd+X+Y.H^{v_{\mathrm D}\leftarrow q_X}=\frac{K_d+Y}{K_d+X+Y},\qquad H^{v_{\mathrm D}\leftarrow q_Y}=\frac{K_d+X}{K_d+X+Y}.

At a positive steady state, the state balance-order matrix and steady output gain are

HA=(−HvD←qX−HvD←qY0−1),dlog⁡qX∗dlog⁡u=1−HvD←qYHvD←qX=Y∗Kd+Y∗.H^A=\begin{pmatrix}-H^{v_{\mathrm D}\leftarrow q_X}&-H^{v_{\mathrm D}\leftarrow q_Y}\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \frac{d\log q_X^*}{d\log u}=\frac{1-H^{v_{\mathrm D}\leftarrow q_Y}}{H^{v_{\mathrm D}\leftarrow q_X}}=\frac{Y^*}{K_d+Y^*}.

Both diagonal entries of HAH^A are negative. Every positive turnover-time choice therefore preserves local stability. Total-output adaptation requires Y∗≪KdY^*\ll K_d. With a small catalytic load, free output also lies below KdK_d, so the two removal orders approach (1,1)(1,1) and the bilinear example in section 6 applies. Larger input raises free controller and moves the orders toward (1,0)(1,0). Stability persists while cancellation fails. The zero-gain limit is the whole upper edge of the triangle, with positive output order. The chosen small catalytic load places the trajectory near the corner (1,1)(1,1).

Free output and total output have different exact steady responses. A finite equilibrium requires k2/γ>k1,D/kcatk_2/\gamma>k_{1,\mathrm D}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}. The balances then give

CXY∗=k1,Dkcatu,Y∗=(k2γ−k1,Dkcat)u,X∗=Kdk1,D/kcatk2/γ−k1,D/kcat.C_{XY}^*=\frac{k_{1,\mathrm D}}{k_{\mathrm{cat}}}u,\quad Y^*=\left(\frac{k_2}{\gamma}-\frac{k_{1,\mathrm D}}{k_{\mathrm{cat}}}\right)u,\quad X^*=K_d\frac{k_{1,\mathrm D}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}}{k_2/\gamma-k_{1,\mathrm D}/k_{\mathrm{cat}}}.

Free X∗X^* is exactly constant for this model and removal rule. Total qX∗=X∗+CXY∗q_X^*=X^*+C_{XY}^* includes an input-dependent bound pool. Its adaptation is approximate at finite concentrations. The animation displays both readouts to make that distinction visible.

Repression removes active promoter from the production flux. Keep the promoter total qGq_G fixed. Binding is G+Y⇌k−k+CGYG+Y\xrightleftharpoons[k_-]{k_+}C_{GY}. Production and output removal are composite processes with the rate laws

q˙X=vR−δqX,vR=k1,RuGqG,qG=G+CGY,qY=Y+CGY,KdCGY=GY.\dot q_X=v_{\mathrm R}-\delta q_X,\quad v_{\mathrm R}=k_{1,\mathrm R}u\frac{G}{q_G},\quad q_G=G+C_{GY},\quad q_Y=Y+C_{GY},\quad K_dC_{GY}=GY.

The free promoter's orders form a different attainable region. Differentiating the two conservation laws gives

HG←qG=1+CGYKd+G+Y,HG←qY=−qYKd+G+Y.H^{G\leftarrow q_G}=1+\frac{C_{GY}}{K_d+G+Y},\qquad H^{G\leftarrow q_Y}=-\frac{q_Y}{K_d+G+Y}.
HG←qG>1,0<HG←qG+HG←qY<1.H^{G\leftarrow q_G}>1,\qquad 0<H^{G\leftarrow q_G}+H^{G\leftarrow q_Y}<1.

The region is an unbounded strip between two sloping lines. A fixed promoter total selects a curve within that region. In this implementation the direct input multiplies production. It does not change the promoter total. Therefore HvR←u=1H^{v_{\mathrm R}\leftarrow u}=1 and HvR←qY=HG←qYH^{v_{\mathrm R}\leftarrow q_Y}=H^{G\leftarrow q_Y}.

High controller abundance makes the two input paths cancel. At a positive steady state,

HA=(−1HG←qY0−1),dlog⁡qX∗dlog⁡u=1+HG←qY.H^A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&H^{G\leftarrow q_Y}\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \frac{d\log q_X^*}{d\log u}=1+H^{G\leftarrow q_Y}.

The state balance-order matrix again remains stable for every positive turnover-time choice. When qY≫max⁡(Kd,qG)q_Y\gg\max(K_d,q_G), free controller wins its total and binding wins the promoter total. Then G≃KdqG/qYG\simeq K_dq_G/q_Y and HG←qY≃−1H^{G\leftarrow q_Y}\simeq-1. Production becomes proportional to u/qYu/q_Y, giving approximate total-output adaptation. A large input decrease leaves that regime. Free promoter recovers and production follows the input.

Promoter titration can give a zero gain at one point without an adaptive range. If the promoter pool is large, HG←qYH^{G\leftarrow q_Y} can pass below minus one and later approach minus one from below. The steady output then rises and falls. A single zero gain, or agreement between two endpoints of a finite step, does not establish restoration throughout the intervening input range. Keep the whole order trajectory and concentration conditions visible.

Both implementations use the same input and output blocks. For the readout y=qXy=q_X, the positive input drives the two synthesis branches at order one:

Hb=(11),Hc=(10),Hd=0.H^b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad H^c=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad H^d=0.

The two state balance-order matrices supply the different cancellation conditions. The triangle and promoter-order region explain why degradation loses total-output adaptation at high controller abundance, whereas repression loses it at low controller abundance. Finite affinity makes these operating ranges approximate. Exact cancellation over a range belongs to the limiting monomial laws, or to a separately proved exact readout such as free XX above.

The colored regions test steady input cancellation. During an animation, the moving point reports the current binding orders. The gain formula applies at a balanced equilibrium. The final point can be tested against the colored region. Crossing that region during a transient does not bound the current output error.

The input implementation determines the adaptive stripe

The earlier animated illustration uses an active input complex whose total changes with the disturbance in its repression design. Its cancellation condition is the sum of the direct and indirect production orders approaching zero. Here the promoter total is fixed and the direct input factor has order one. The condition is consequently 1+HG←qY≃01+H^{G\leftarrow q_Y}\simeq0. The two pictures use the same binding geometry with different input specifications.

Specify the binding mechanism, controller removal, input and readout before testing adaptation. Reaction orders reveal both cancellation and its failure. Local stability alone does not restore the output.

Optional calculations

These calculations support the main route and sit outside its 95-minute clock.

A1 · Why ordinary stability is weaker than D-stability

One stable matrix can become unstable when its rows acquire different clocks. Take

H=(12−2−3),D=(4001).H=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-2&-3\end{pmatrix},\qquad D=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.

The matrix HH has trace minus two and determinant one, so both eigenvalues are minus one. The matrix DHDH has trace one and determinant four. Its eigenvalues have real part one half. Stability of HH therefore does not guarantee D-stability.

The diagonal certificate avoids this problem. Because diagonal PP and Λτ∗−1\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1} commute, differentiation of V=zqTΛτ∗PzqV=z_q^{\mathsf T}\Lambda_{\tau^*}Pz_q gives V˙=zqT(HTP+PH)zq\dot V=z_q^{\mathsf T}(H^{\mathsf T}P+PH)z_q. Both positivity of VV and strict negativity of its derivative hold for every positive turnover vector.

A2 · Why the input-output determinant gives the output response

Eliminate the input column's state component using a block matrix of determinant one:

[HAHbHcHd][I−(HA)−1Hb01]=[HA0HcHd−Hc(HA)−1Hb].\begin{bmatrix}H^A&H^b\\H^c&H^d\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I&-(H^A)^{-1}H^b\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}H^A&0\\H^c&H^d-H^c(H^A)^{-1}H^b\end{bmatrix}.

Taking determinants gives the condition in section 6. The argument requires a nonsingular state balance-order matrix. Remove fixed conservation constraints before linearizing. A singularity at a bifurcation requires a different local analysis.

The relative and absolute input-output systems differ only by reference scales. For the same biomolecular model,

A=Λq∗Λτ∗−1HAΛq∗−1,b=1w∗Λq∗Λτ∗−1Hb,c=y∗HcΛq∗−1,d=y∗w∗Hd.\begin{aligned}A&=\Lambda_{q^*}\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H^A\Lambda_{q^*}^{-1},&b&=\frac{1}{w^*}\Lambda_{q^*}\Lambda_{\tau^*}^{-1}H^b,\\c&=y^*H^c\Lambda_{q^*}^{-1},&d&=\frac{y^*}{w^*}H^d.\end{aligned}

The steady gain in absolute units is (y∗/w∗)[Hd−Hc(HA)−1Hb](y^*/w^*)[H^d-H^c(H^A)^{-1}H^b]. Both coordinate descriptions therefore give the same zero-gain condition.

A3 · Unequal turnover times in the repressilator

The smooth repressilator has a unique positive equilibrium. Each steady concentration is the same decreasing function of its predecessor. Three substitutions make the first concentration a fixed point of a strictly decreasing scalar function. It therefore has at most one solution. The symmetric positive solution exists, so it is the unique equilibrium.

The equal-clock condition matters to the instability threshold. Write the fold-change matrix as D(−I−gR)D(-I-gR), with D=diag⁡(d1,d2,d3)D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2,d_3) and positive turnover rates did_i. Its characteristic polynomial is

s3+(d1+d2+d3)s2+(d1d2+d2d3+d3d1)s+(1+g3)d1d2d3.s^3+(d_1+d_2+d_3)s^2+(d_1d_2+d_2d_3+d_3d_1)s+(1+g^3)d_1d_2d_3.

The cubic Routh–Hurwitz criterion gives stability precisely when

(d1+d2+d3)(d1d2+d2d3+d3d1)>(1+g3)d1d2d3.(d_1+d_2+d_3)(d_1d_2+d_2d_3+d_3d_1)>(1+g^3)d_1d_2d_3.

Equal rates reduce the inequality to g<2g\lt2. Unequal rates can stabilize a state with g>2g>2. The repressilator example is therefore a conditional oscillation mechanism, not a guarantee for all positive clocks.

The main trajectory was integrated with α=100\alpha=100, n=3n=3 and equal unit turnover times, starting from a small nonsymmetric perturbation. At a late upward crossing of the first concentration through its equilibrium value, integrating one measured period returns to the same state with relative error below 10−810^{-8}. The computed Floquet multipliers are approximately 1, 0.0075, 01,\ 0.0075,\ 0. The unit multiplier is the phase direction. The other two indicate transverse attraction of this numerical periodic orbit.

A4 · Recover the one-pair formula from the general inverse

Choose x=(E,S,CES)Tx=(E,S,C_{ES})^{\mathsf T}, q=(qE,qS)Tq=(q_E,q_S)^{\mathsf T} and the association equilibrium constant k=1/Kdk=1/K_d. The matrices are

L=(101011),N=(−1−11).L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad N=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}.

The stacked derivative is

(E/qE0CES/qE0S/qSCES/qS−1−11).\begin{pmatrix}E/q_E&0&C_{ES}/q_E\\0&S/q_S&C_{ES}/q_S\\-1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}.

The last row of its inverse gives the complex's orders. Its first two entries reproduce the displayed total-concentration formulas. A single catalytic flux kcatCESk_{\mathrm{cat}}C_{ES} has the same total-concentration orders when kcatk_{\mathrm{cat}} is fixed. A sum of catalytic contributions instead has their flux-weighted orders.

A5 · Every interior point of the triangle is attainable

Take positive weights a,b,ca,b,c with a+b+c=1a+b+c=1 for the vertices (1,1),(1,0),(0,1)(1,1),(1,0),(0,1). At any fixed Kd>0K_d>0, choose

S=Kdba,E=Kdca,CES=ESKd.S=K_d\frac{b}{a},\qquad E=K_d\frac{c}{a},\qquad C_{ES}=\frac{ES}{K_d}.

The positive totals qE=E+CESq_E=E+C_{ES} and qS=S+CESq_S=S+C_{ES} realize those weights. This proves attainability, in addition to containment. The barycentric weights describe the order decomposition. They are not the fractions carrying either molecular total.
